look_here_first: GIANT CUTGRASS: native emergent warm-season rhizomatous wetland grass with tall reedlike jointed leafy stems, broad rough/sharp blades, and a tall open branching inflorescence rather than Phragmites' feathery plume. Confirm a separate male/female spikelet structure with magnification and true leaf collar; do not identify by wet habitat or blade sharpness alone.

what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: Tall rooted marsh stand with culm and rhizome where excavation allowed
Rough leaf edge with true ligule magnified (avoid cutting hands)
Mature male versus female spikelets in large open panicle
Side-by-side Phragmites and Leersia without disturbance
crew_field_check: Phragmites australis can have taller dense feathery heads and includes BOTH native and introduced lineages, so do not call Phragmites invasive by appearance alone. Texas wild-rice (*Zizania texana*) is a rare protected true aquatic San Marcos River endemic and very different from emergent giant cutgrass. Rice cutgrass (*Leersia oryzoides*) is smaller and has slender flattened rice-like spikelets.
Original Florida photograph is not a Hays specimen voucher; preserve county-range status.
